bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Innovative hub-and-spoke model: large central hubs act as main centres for secondary, tertiary and top-level specialty care while spokes serve nearby regions, improving bed utilisation, balancing service mix and keeping costs in check
- Strong brand identity in pediatric healthcare, drawing patients and doctor recommendations across regions and building deep trust and loyalty so families return for all their healthcare needs
- Excellence in pediatric and perinatal care with expert services in neurology, nephrology, oncology and cardiology; skill in blending children's and newborn care sets it apart and gives a clear market edge
- Child-centric healthcare framework - friendly hospital spaces and staff specially trained to comfort children, leading to better treatment results and happier patients
- Collaborative multi-disciplinary approach bringing pediatrics, neurology, nephrology, oncology and cardiology experts together with nurses, therapists and admin staff for personalized treatment plans
- Strategic doctor engagement: over 1,050+ full-time doctors on retainer for 24/7 consultant-led care (elsewhere stated as over 910 full-time doctors), many with advanced training from the UK, USA, Canada and Australia
- Runs India's largest private pediatric Diplomate of National Board (DNB) training program with postgraduate and fellowship spots, building a pipeline of future specialists
- Integrated mother-and-child ecosystem creating seamless care from pregnancy through neonatal stages to advanced pediatric needs, boosting patient loyalty and positioning Rainbow as a top referral centre for critical cases
- COSO-aligned risk management framework with Risk Management Committee oversight and compliance training
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Medical ethics, legal and regulatory compliance — Operating in a highly regulated sector requires consistent compliance with healthcare, labour, environmental, data and anti-corruption requirements; any breach can affect licenses, reputation and operating flexibility. Mitigated through a strengthened code of conduct, compliance training, whistle-blower mechanisms, internal controls, policy reviews, ethics oversight and periodic legal/compliance audits. Flagged as having negative financial implications.
- Privacy, cybersecurity and data security — Hospitals handle sensitive patient and employee data; any unauthorised access, leak or cyber incident can result in legal exposure, regulatory scrutiny, service disruption and loss of trust. Mitigated via access controls, encryption, privileged-access management, backup and recovery protocols, vendor safeguards, awareness training, incident response and regular security audits. Negative financial implications.
- Occupational health and safety of clinical staff — Clinical staff face exposure to infections, sharps injuries, chemicals, radiation, patient-handling risks and fire/emergency hazards; a strong safety culture is essential to protect employees and ensure uninterrupted patient care. Mitigated through infection prevention and control protocols, PPE, safety training, emergency drills, incident reporting, root-cause review, vaccination support, ergonomic controls and periodic health surveillance. Negative financial implications.
- Water and waste management (hazardous and non-hazardous) — Healthcare facilities generate biomedical, hazardous and domestic waste and are significant users of water; weak segregation, treatment or reuse practices can lead to non-compliance, reputational damage, infection risk and higher operating cost. Mitigated through strict segregation and labeling, authorised disposal via approved vendors, wastewater treatment and reuse, rainwater harvesting where feasible, 3R practices and periodic audits against pollution control requirements. Negative financial implications.
- Responsible procurement and supply chain resilience — Uninterrupted availability of medicines, consumables, diagnostics and equipment is critical in healthcare; poor supplier governance or concentration risk can affect service delivery and cost stability. Mitigation includes supplier due diligence, quality and ethical sourcing checks, critical inventory planning and an alternate sourcing strategy. Negative financial implications.
- Enterprise risk management and business continuity — The healthcare business is exposed to operational, clinical, regulatory, technology, supply and external shocks; a structured risk management framework is needed to reduce disruption and protect continuity of care. Mitigated by enterprise risk registers, mitigation-plan reviews with stakeholders, monitoring of critical dependencies, stress-testing of business continuity and disaster recovery plans, and periodic management reviews. Negative financial implications.
- Talent attraction, retention and high employee attrition — Healthcare quality depends on the availability of skilled doctors, nurses, technicians and support staff. The BRSR discloses a permanent-employee turnover rate of 37% in FY2026 (34% male, 40% female), up from 35% in FY2025 and 33% in FY2024, with the Company noting FY2025-26 attrition data includes nursing exits with tenure of less than 3 months - a structural workforce-churn exposure for a consultant-led clinical model.
- Single-activity and geographic concentration — 100% of turnover comes from a single activity - human health activities / medical services (healthcare services) - and operations are confined to six states in India with no international locations and no export revenue, leaving the Company undiversified by both business line and geography.
- Energy intensity of hospital operations — Hospital operations are energy-intensive because of continuous clinical services, critical equipment, HVAC loads, lighting and imaging systems; the Company frames improving energy efficiency as an opportunity (positive implications) addressed through energy audits, LED retrofits, smart metering, HVAC optimisation, preventive maintenance, renewable energy sourcing where feasible and site-level monitoring of utility intensity.

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers

business.body:
- "Rainbow is currently the country's largest pediatric hospital chain with 24 hospitals spread across 9 cities", founded 1999 by Dr. Ramesh Kancharla, with the network described as the "Largest chain of comprehensive pediatric care with cutting-edge quaternary care services".
- Accreditation is the stated quality moat: "Country's first pediatric hospital to have 2 flagship hub hospitals, one each in Hyderabad and Bengaluru, awarded with JCI Accreditation", plus "Country's first standalone fertility center BirthRight Fertility, Kondapur, Hyderabad" re-accredited by JCI; 14 hospitals are NABH-accredited and 3 JCI-accredited.
- The operating model is presented as four distinctive elements - "Focused child centric healthcare network", "Multi-disciplinary approach", "Hub and Spoke model for wider city coverage" and a "Unique doctor engagement model" of "Full-time, 24/7 consultant-led service".
- Training is positioned as a talent moat: "the country's largest pediatric DNB training programme in private healthcare", recognised as an MRCPCH Examination Centre and as a training centre by the National Board of Examinations, backed by "1075+ full-time doctors" many "trained or possess qualifications from the UK, USA, Canada, Australia".
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Acquisitions] The 2025-2026 phase covers the "Acquisition of: Prashanthi Hospital, Warangal & Pratiksha Hospital, Guwahati", with footnotes dating Prashanthi (100 beds) to 1st July 2025 within Telangana and the Guwahati 150 beds to "acquisition & integration of Pratiksha Hospital, Guwahati from 1st September 2025"; both sit in the "New Hospitals" (under 5 years) bucket.
- [Doctor model] Doctors "work exclusively on a full-time, retainer basis" in teams with a 24/7 commitment, supported by "Retainer/Support in beginning years", competitive compensation and absorption into the network - the stated source of "High retention and loyalty" and support for pediatric retrieval services.
- [Ownership] Shareholding as on June 30, 2026: Promoter & Promoter Group 49.8%, MFs & AIFs 19.9%, FPIs & NRIs 16.0%, Others 14.3%; institutional holders above 1% include ICICI Prudential & ISIF Equity Fund (5.9%), DSP Mutual Fund (4.1%), Franklin Templeton Investment Funds (2.9%), Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (2.1%) and Vanguard Fund (1.9%).
- [Clinical capability] The appendix details capability the deck presents as competitive depth: a pediatric ECMO retrieval team that travelled ~1,800 km to Guwahati for "the first reported pediatric ECMO transfer out of Northeast India" (child on ECMO 36 days, discharged in good health); multi-organ trauma management after a five-storey fall; a hemispherotomy for drug-refractory epilepsy; and a chronic Caesarean Scar Ectopic Pregnancy repair - the ECMO case framed as "expanding the addressable referral base and reinforcing the hospital's role as a national escalation point for pediatric critical care".
- [Capex character] The deck notes "Allocation of significant portion of capex towards interiors of hospitals for creating congenial environment", tying spend to the child-centric design premise, but gives no capex amount.
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: Founded in 1998 and headquartered in Hyderabad, Rainbow operates a network of 24 hospitals and 5 clinics across 9 cities with over 2,435 beds dedicated to child-centric care. Pediatric services form the backbone, covering newborn and pediatric intensive care (PICU/NICU), multi-specialty treatments and advanced quaternary care such as multi-organ transplants, while Birthright handles routine and complex obstetric care, fetal medicine, perinatal genetics, IVF and gynecology. The Company serves children, mothers and families through an asset-light hub-and-spoke model, with about 50% of pediatric cases arriving as emergencies.

outlook.body:
- Replicate the success of the Hyderabad flagship referral centre at the Bengaluru, Chennai, Gurugram and Guwahati flagship centres over the next five years, with the hub-and-spoke network and regional spoke hospitals complementing and accelerating growth of these referral centres
- Expand not merely to increase capacity but to make specialized women's and children's healthcare more accessible: strengthen South India leadership across Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu; build a meaningful presence across the National Capital Region and its surrounding growth corridors in North India; and pursue planned developments in Western and Central India
- Pursue inorganic growth alongside organic expansion, evaluating acquisition opportunities that complement the clinical model, strengthen regional presence and create long-term value, with the same discipline and prudence applied historically
- 'One Rainbow' - build a unified clinical model with standardized care pathways, evidence-based protocols, robust governance and continuous quality improvement across every hospital, so scaling never compromises quality of care
- Build a connected digital ecosystem anchored on the One Rainbow Digital Platform - a single integrated gateway spanning appointments, diagnostics, teleconsultations, pregnancy care, fertility services, vaccination programs and long-term pediatric health management, supported by AI-enabled tools and an integrated technology architecture
- Strengthen the specialized neonatal and pediatric transport program as a core differentiator, expanding its reach to make referral centres more accessible to families across the country
- Scale academics and training to build a sustainable pipeline of specialists trained 'in the Rainbow way', reinforcing future clinical capability while supplying skilled talent to the country
- Rainbow Skill CSR initiative - establish advanced simulation-based training centres for doctors, nurses and allied healthcare professionals, starting with the first centre in Hyderabad and extending the model to other larger networks in future
- With a significant phase of planned capacity additions now operational, shift focus to driving higher utilization, enhancing operating performance and delivering sustainable growth, while continuing to evaluate expansion opportunities in line with evolving market demand
- Improve occupancy and asset utilization across recently commissioned and acquired hospitals as a key strategic focus
- Enhance sales and marketing capabilities, strengthen doctor engagement and expand the shared care network to improve market reach, reinforce specialty-led growth and support sustainable patient volumes over the long term
- In accordance with Regulation 43A of the SEBI Listing Regulations the Board has formulated and adopted a Dividend Distribution Policy setting out the key principles guiding the Board and management on declaration and distribution of dividend; the policy is published on the Company's website. The Company states it has consistently declared and paid dividends to equity shareholders, and for FY2025-26 the Directors have recommended a final dividend of Rs 3.5 per equity share of face value Rs 10 each for shareholder approval at the 28th AGM (record date July 21, 2026), against Rs 3 per share declared for each of FY2023-24 and FY2024-25 and Rs 2 per share for FY2021-22. For the year under review no amount is proposed to be transferred to any Reserve of the Company. At Board level, capital deployment is governed by two dedicated committees: the Business Strategy & Investment Committee reviews strategic growth opportunities, expansion initiatives, investments, acquisitions and capital deployment decisions to support sustainable growth and long-term value creation, while the Treasury Management Committee reviews investment strategy, liquidity, debt position, interest rate exposure and capital allocation to support disciplined financial management. Structured Board oversight extends to strategy, growth initiatives, risk management, ESG priorities and capital allocation. Management describes the year's network expansion as having strengthened the Company's ability to deploy capital efficiently across established and emerging markets, and states that the successful integration and strong performance of recent acquisitions reinforces confidence in pursuing similar opportunities with the same discipline and prudence.

- Occupational health and safety programme covering infection prevention and control protocols, PPE use, safety training, emergency drills, incident reporting, root-cause review, vaccination support, ergonomic controls and periodic health surveillance
- Service quality, clinical outcomes and patient safety treated as a material ESG opportunity, supported by clinical audits, standard treatment protocols, infection control, patient feedback loops, quality committees, sentinel-event review, accreditation adherence and outcome tracking
- Diversity, equity and inclusion: women constitute 62% of total employees (3,951 of 6,397), 58% of permanent employees, 33% of Key Management Personnel and 14% of the Board of Directors; the Company commits to equitable hiring and promotion practices, inclusion initiatives, grievance redressal, anti-harassment measures and leadership accountability

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Rainbow has grown into a network of 24 hospitals and 5 clinics across 9 cities, offering over 2,435 beds, expanded through an asset-light hub-and-spoke model. Large hub hospitals of around 200 plus beds (described elsewhere as at least 150 beds) at Banjara Hills (Hyderabad), Marathahalli (Bengaluru), Guindy (Chennai) and Malviya Nagar (Delhi) serve as centres for tertiary and quaternary care with specialized PICU/NICU units, while spoke hospitals of mostly 70+ beds (minimum 50 beds) provide secondary and tertiary services in nearby regions without full duplication of high-end facilities - a setup that improves bed utilization, balances service mix and cuts operational costs. Recent expansions include new units in Anna Nagar (Chennai), Rajahmundry, Electronic City, HRBR, Mahadevapura IVF, Warangal and Guwahati, and the model supports scalability with ongoing projects in Gurugram, Electronic City, Pune, Segualli and others. During FY2025-26 the Company completed two hospital acquisitions, expanding its geographic footprint and capacity in line with its growth strategy; post year-end it further strengthened the network by operationalising new hospital locations and launching an IVF centre, which management expects to support volume growth and improved infrastructure utilisation over the medium term. Management states that the expansion of the network during the year increased the operating base and strengthened the Company's ability to deploy capital efficiently across established and emerging markets, and that the operational expansion initiatives are expected to contribute to improved operational efficiencies, higher throughput and greater revenue visibility. Forward plans emphasise optimising existing units, targeted Tier II expansions via clinical models, IVF/maternity growth, an international push and M&A. No project-wise capex outlay, commissioning date or bed-addition schedule is disclosed in this section.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management expects new hospitals maturing and strengthened digital capabilities driving patient engagement to position Rainbow to reinforce its leadership in specialized women's and children's healthcare
- A significant phase of planned capacity additions is now operational, so the near-term lever is higher utilization and occupancy rather than fresh capacity, particularly across recently commissioned and acquired hospitals
- Successful integration and strong performance of recent acquisitions has reinforced management confidence in pursuing similar opportunities
- The consultant-led model, deep expertise in pediatrics and perinatal care and commitment of teams across the network are cited by the CEO as the standout operating strengths
- India's real GDP growth for FY2026-27 is projected between 6.8% and 7.2% (Crisil forecasts 6.6%), supported by government infrastructure spending, steadily rising private investment and a reliable services growth path
- India's healthcare expenditure was 3.3% of GDP in 2023, among the lowest in the world, with per capita healthcare expenditure of $84.7 - only 11.1% of China's - indicating a structurally under-served market
- India lags the global average in hospital bed availability against the IPHS desirable benchmark of 20 beds per 10,000 population (10 beds per 10,000 the minimum essential standard)
- Structural demand drivers cited for India: demographic dividend (working-age population of 849.9 million in 2023, peaking at 967.7 million in 2034), rising urbanization (urban population to reach 567.7 million by 2030, 37.2% of total) and growing per capita income (CAGR of 6.6% between FY2023 and FY2026)
- Private consumption continues to anchor India's economic growth, with PFCE growth of 7.7% between FY2025 and FY2026 supported by GST rate rationalization, stable employment and rising real purchasing power
- Downside risks to the macro outlook include escalation of geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, a reevaluation of AI profit expectations leading to lower investment, abrupt financial-market correction, and larger fiscal deficits pressuring long-term interest rates

risks.note: Operating in a highly regulated sector requires consistent compliance with healthcare, labour, environmental, data and anti-corruption requirements; any breach can affect licenses, reputation and operating flexibility. Mitigated through a strengthened code of conduct, compliance training, whistle-blower mechanisms, internal controls, policy reviews, ethics oversight and periodic legal/compliance audits. Flagged as having negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Medical ethics, legal and regulatory compliance

risks.note: Hospitals handle sensitive patient and employee data; any unauthorised access, leak or cyber incident can result in legal exposure, regulatory scrutiny, service disruption and loss of trust. Mitigated via access controls, encryption, privileged-access management, backup and recovery protocols, vendor safeguards, awareness training, incident response and regular security audits. Negative financial implications.

Clinical staff face exposure to infections, sharps injuries, chemicals, radiation, patient-handling risks and fire/emergency hazards; a strong safety culture is essential to protect employees and ensure uninterrupted patient care. Mitigated through infection prevention and control protocols, PPE, safety training, emergency drills, incident reporting, root-cause review, vaccination support, ergonomic controls and periodic health surveillance. Negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Occupational health and safety of clinical staff

risks.note: Healthcare facilities generate biomedical, hazardous and domestic waste and are significant users of water; weak segregation, treatment or reuse practices can lead to non-compliance, reputational damage, infection risk and higher operating cost. Mitigated through strict segregation and labeling, authorised disposal via approved vendors, wastewater treatment and reuse, rainwater harvesting where feasible, 3R practices and periodic audits against pollution control requirements. Negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Water and waste management (hazardous and non-hazardous)

risks.note: Uninterrupted availability of medicines, consumables, diagnostics and equipment is critical in healthcare; poor supplier governance or concentration risk can affect service delivery and cost stability. Mitigation includes supplier due diligence, quality and ethical sourcing checks, critical inventory planning and an alternate sourcing strategy. Negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Responsible procurement and supply chain resilience

risks.note: The healthcare business is exposed to operational, clinical, regulatory, technology, supply and external shocks; a structured risk management framework is needed to reduce disruption and protect continuity of care. Mitigated by enterprise risk registers, mitigation-plan reviews with stakeholders, monitoring of critical dependencies, stress-testing of business continuity and disaster recovery plans, and periodic management reviews. Negative financial implications.
risks.risk: Enterprise risk management and business continuity

risks.note: Healthcare quality depends on the availability of skilled doctors, nurses, technicians and support staff. The BRSR discloses a permanent-employee turnover rate of 37% in FY2026 (34% male, 40% female), up from 35% in FY2025 and 33% in FY2024, with the Company noting FY2025-26 attrition data includes nursing exits with tenure of less than 3 months - a structural workforce-churn exposure for a consultant-led clinical model.
risks.risk: Talent attraction, retention and high employee attrition

risks.note: 100% of turnover comes from a single activity - human health activities / medical services (healthcare services) - and operations are confined to six states in India with no international locations and no export revenue, leaving the Company undiversified by both business line and geography.

meta.thesis: Rainbow delivered record Q4 revenue (INR 460cr, +24% YoY) and PAT (+38% YoY) driven by 500 bed additions and recovering occupancies, with management guiding for 20% growth in FY27 fueled by a massive 900-bed pipeline (Gurugram, Coimbatore, Pune) and a strategic pivot to reduce seasonality via super-specialty mix and fertility expansion.
